claims.text: A random atomic distribution in near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles produces severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion generates local energy barriers that slow atomic diffusion.
Severe lattice distortion inhibits grain-boundary mobility.
Reduced diffusion and grain-boundary mobility preserve nanoparticle structural and chemical integrity at elevated temperatures.
Near-equiatomic multi-element solid solutions can retain structural stability within at least part of the stated elevated-temperature range.
Rapid quenching locks nanoparticles into a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles have high lattice distortion.
A moderate post-synthesis anneal can partially relax lattice distortion without inducing phase separation.
The degree of lattice distortion and atomic-scale compositional homogeneity mediate high-temperature stability.
Relaxing lattice distortion lowers local barriers to atomic mobility.
Lower atomic-mobility barriers accelerate diffusion, grain growth, or phase segregation during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
Unannealed, highly distorted nanoparticles will undergo less grain growth than annealed nanoparticles under identical high-temperature exposure.
Unannealed, highly distorted nanoparticles will undergo less phase segregation than annealed nanoparticles under identical high-temperature exposure.
Unannealed nanoparticles will retain greater chemical stability than annealed nanoparticles under identical high-temperature exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to near-equiatomic, rapidly quenched nanoparticles whose stability is governed by intrinsic lattice distortion.
Secondary phases, contamination, or dominant surface-energy effects can make the proposed lattice-distortion mechanism inapplicable.

Failure of annealed nanoparticles to exhibit significantly faster grain growth, phase segregation, or chemical degradation than the unannealed control would falsify lattice distortion as the primary stability mediator.
